Chapter One: How White Supremacy Became Part of Everyday Life.
You know, it’s tempting to think that history’s all about those big, dramatic moments—marches, powerful speeches, maybe a landmark court decision. But honestly? Most of what shapes our lives happens quietly, almost invisibly, woven into the routines of everyday life. When we talk about white supremacy in America, it’s not just the obvious outbursts of hatred or violence. It’s really about those subtle, persistent ideas that have soaked into the fabric of society—shaping what folks expect, what they fear, and what they believe is possible.
Picture this: in small towns and big cities alike, families gather around dinner tables, swapping stories about their day. Maybe someone talks about work, or how things went at school. And sometimes, without anyone even noticing, old ideas about who belongs—and who doesn’t—just slip right into the conversation. A parent warns their child to be careful in a certain neighborhood. Or maybe a teacher, without meaning to, expects a little less from a student just because of their background. These moments, they don’t feel dramatic. But they stack up, and over time, they shape how we see ourselves and each other.
The roots of white supremacy in America run deep—way back to the earliest days of colonization. Early settlers arrived with dreams of a new life, sure, but also with some pretty powerful beliefs about who deserved power… and who didn’t. Over generations, those beliefs hardened into laws and everyday habits, justifying things like the enslavement of millions and the forced removal of whole communities. Even when the most blatant forms of oppression were finally challenged, the core ideas stuck around, always finding new ways to show up.
Most people don’t wake up thinking about “ideology.” They’re just trying to pay the bills, get through the workday, or keep their kids safe. But here’s the thing: the rules that decide who gets a good job, who feels welcome in a neighborhood, or even who’s treated fairly by the police—those rules are shaped by ideas that have been handed down for generations. And it’s not just about individual prejudice. These ideas are actually baked into the systems that keep society running.
Imagine a young worker, frustrated after being overlooked for a promotion. What if she doesn’t realize that the company’s hiring practices were set up decades ago—by people who only saw certain folks as “management material”? Or think about a family looking for a new home, not knowing that the neighborhood they can actually afford was once off-limits to people who looked like them. Even the people who benefit from these systems sometimes feel uneasy, like something’s just not right, even if they’re not sure why.
Over time, it’s become clear: white supremacy isn’t just about individual attitudes. It’s a system—a whole set of rules, policies, and expectations that decide who gets ahead and who’s left behind. And this system? It’s so deeply built in that a lot of folks barely notice it, even when they’re the ones being hurt by it. People just get used to thinking, “That’s just the way it is,” not realizing these patterns were created on purpose, and kept alive for a reason.
And this persistence—it’s not an accident. Throughout history, folks in power have found ways to adapt. The language changes, but the basic structure stays the same. When one kind of discrimination gets challenged, another quietly takes its place. Laws get rewritten, but those old assumptions hang on. That’s why progress can feel so slow—every step forward seems to bring new obstacles, new reasons to keep things as they are.
But here’s something important: even as these systems continue, there are always people who notice the cracks. Maybe it’s a teacher who refuses to lower expectations for any student. Or a neighbor who goes out of their way to welcome newcomers. Or a worker who calls out unfair rules at their job. These small acts of resistance—they’re the seeds of change. They’re reminders that our world isn’t set in stone, and the ideas shaping it can be questioned—and changed.
So, the story of white supremacy in America isn’t just about what happened long ago. It’s about the choices people make every day—often without even realizing it. It’s about how old ideas keep shaping new realities, and how, by noticing and questioning these patterns, we really can build a different future.
